bone-coral-editorial-cinematic-dark-hero.title: bone + coral · editorial · cinematic dark hero
bone-coral-editorial-cinematic-dark-hero.universal_prompt:
This is a restrained, editorial, gallery-style interface built on a strict modular grid, a near-monochrome palette, and a single saturated accent. The overall gestalt is "quiet dark room with one bright object on a plinth" — calm, deliberate, contemplative, where the system does most of the talking and one element does the singing.

The direction is editorial. The design is trying to make the viewer slow down and look, to read rather than scan, to treat each section like a page in a magazine rather than a feed. The hero strategy is a single fixed full-color media block anchoring one side of the screen, with a tall text block balancing it on the other, everything else dimmed into a near-monochrome surround so the eye has no choice but to land on the bright thing. Mood is neutral-to-cool overall, warmed only by the accent, and the register stays calm and premium across the entire system.

Color is built from four roles working together. The background is a near-black at roughly #0A0A0A that anchors everything; layered on top of it, a surface tone at roughly #1A1A1A and a muted support tone at roughly #2A2A2A create the tonal separation between blocks without ever resorting to borders. Ink is pure white at #FFFFFF for all primary text and bright elements. A single saturated warm accent at roughly #E83A2E appears only inside the dominant media block and as occasional micro-marks (a small square, a hover state, a subtle underline beneath the heading), and nowhere else. Contrast logic is brightness-driven: critical text is white-on-near-black with a contrast ratio comfortably above WCAG AAA, while secondary blocks are dimmed intentionally to a value range that signals "supporting, not central" — they should never carry critical copy because they would not pass contrast tests and should not need to. There are no gradients, no glows, no glass, no bloom, no grain; the only "trick" worth replicating is a tonal under-tint inside the dominant block that makes it feel like a slight light source rather than a flat tile. The discipline of "one accent, one place, one moment" is the spine of the entire system.

Typography uses a single humanist sans-serif family for everything — display, body, labels, and accents — leaning on weight, size, and spacing rather than multiple faces to express hierarchy. The display face sits at roughly 40 to 48 pixels on a desktop viewport, around five to six percent of viewport height, set in a regular-to-medium weight with a touch of extra tracking and a generous 1.3 to 1.4 line-height, giving headings a calm, editorial presence rather than a banner-shout. Body sits around 16 pixels with the same family and similar leading. Accent caps are used sparingly as small uppercase labels with open tracking, often rotated 90 degrees to function as vertical meta-strips, and they remain the same family in a smaller size. There is no separate monospaced face in this system. The scale ratio between display and body is roughly three to one, which keeps display clearly primary without becoming poster-sized. The pairing decision — single family, weight-led hierarchy — is the move; resist the urge to introduce a second face.

Layout and composition are modular and asymmetric, magazine-style, built on an explicit twelve-column grid with consistent gutters. The first screen splits into two dominant zones: a left text block, narrow but vertically tall, and a right media block, roughly square and dominant, separated by a narrow gutter that holds a vertical label. Smaller supporting blocks are stacked toward the left and right edges and bottom, all dimmed to a near-monochrome value. Asymmetric balance is the rule: heavy on the right with the full-color image, counterweighted by tall, restrained text on the left. Negative space is generous and uniform, creating a premium, gallery feel. No clipped large shapes, no bleed images, nothing breaks the grid; alignment is strict throughout. The grid governs everything from the corner navigation anchors down to the pagination dots. On mobile, the right media block should move above the left text block, columns collapse to one, and the vertical rotated label returns to horizontal as a small meta line.

Visual hierarchy reads as a strict numbered ordering. First the eye hits the right-side full-color media block because it is the largest, brightest, and most saturated object on the page. Second it lands on the left-aligned white heading because of its scale and contrast. Third it picks up the small wordmark top-left, the menu marker top-right, and the CTA marker bottom-right, all sitting in the corners as quiet anchors. Fourth it notices the vertical rotated label in the gutter, the pagination dots bottom-left, and the page indicator mid-right. Finally it registers the dimmed supporting blocks as atmosphere rather than content. The page is legible almost instantly because dimmed blocks recede on their own; nothing has to fight for attention because almost everything has been told to step back.

The hero treatment, described in design language, is a single dominant media block functioning as a museum tableau, anchored in the upper-right or right half of the viewport, framed by generous negative space and treated with one saturated accent that lives inside the image itself rather than as an overlay or border. The headline sits opposite it on the left, large and white, with a small subhead and a tiny caption beneath. A vertical rotated label in the narrow gutter between the two main zones functions as a quiet meta-strip, naming the section without competing with the heading. Nothing sits on top of the image; nothing breaks the frame of the image; the image is not a background, it is an object on a plinth. Framing is square or near-square for the dominant block, with a strict rectangular crop, no masks, no rounded corners.

Navigation and wayfinding follow a corner-anchor system. A small wordmark sits top-left, a "Menu" label with a tiny circle indicator sits top-right, and a primary action with a tiny circle indicator sits bottom-right. There is no horizontal nav bar, no full-width menu strip, no breadcrumb. The wayfinding chrome is reduced to micro-dots and small text labels, with the dots acting as a recurring motif — every interactive anchor in the system wears a small circle next to it. Scrollytelling, when used, should be driven by a quiet rhythm: dimmed supporting blocks fade in or lift slightly as they enter the viewport, staggered by 50 to 80 milliseconds between siblings, with the dominant block remaining still so it can breathe. No pinning is needed; the page is one steady, editorial scroll.

Media and imagery follow a single rule: one full-color, full-brightness media block anchors the screen, everything else is either dimmed into a near-monochrome value range or treated as quiet, low-contrast graphic tiles — a grid texture, a flat surface, a cropped detail. The render style of the dominant block is photographic or photographic-feeling, with crisp edges, no overlay text, no duotone, no heavy filter, no grain. Supporting media should be background-level rather than featured. There is no bloom, no glow, no heavy color grading; the only "treatment" is the dimming itself, which uses value rather than desaturation. Crops are uniform rectangles respecting the grid. Real imagery, when used, lives in the dominant block; everywhere else, abstract and quiet wins.

The standout solutions worth replicating in any thematic pivot are these. First, the rule of one accent: a single saturated warm color appears inside the dominant media block and nowhere else on the page, with maybe a micro-mark in the chrome. Second, the corner-anchor navigation system: wordmark top-left, menu top-right, primary action bottom-right, all using the same small circle indicator as a unifying motif. Third, tonal hierarchy without borders: blocks are separated by value contrast on a near-black ground, never by lines, shadows, or glass. Fourth, a vertical rotated label in the narrow gutter that names a section without breaking the grid. Fifth, pagination dots as a quiet state indicator in the bottom-left, with one active and the rest dimmed. Sixth, a small accent square or a thin underline beneath the heading that mirrors the accent inside the main image, tying the two halves of the screen together.

The things to learn from, as generalizable lessons, are these. Let one element carry the color story and let everything else go quiet. Use the grid as a strict invariant and never break it. Reserve the brightest, most saturated, largest block for the thing you most want seen and dim everything else into support. Pair every interactive anchor with a small dot or marker so the system has a recurring visual motif. Treat typography as a hierarchy of size and weight within a single family rather than a parade of faces. And let motion be editorial — slow, sequential, opacity-led — so the system feels like turning a page rather than launching an app.

The watch-outs, as reusable caveats rather than complaints, are these. When you have a single saturated accent in a near-monochrome field, that accent will vibrate against any other warm element in the same hue family, so kill any incidental warmth in supporting blocks. Dimmed blocks are at risk of disappearing entirely; lift them just enough to read as background, never so much that they compete. Small circle indicators are almost always too small for comfortable touch targets, so inflate the hit area to at least 44 pixels even when the visible dot is tiny. Vertical rotated labels lose their meaning on small screens unless you rotate them back to horizontal, so plan a responsive treatment from the start. Dimmed text below WCAG contrast thresholds is a trap; never place critical copy on dimmed blocks. A single full-color image will crowd if you surround it with busy graphic tiles, so keep the supporting tiles flat and quiet. Pagination dots need stronger active-versus-inactive differentiation than value alone, so add a position change or a fill. And finally, never animate scale above roughly 1.02 on a system this restrained, because any aggressive motion will shatter the gallery stillness the whole palette is working to create.

A pagination or section counter — typically a tiny two-digit step marker — sits somewhere along the top edge to signal that this is the first of a small sequence of pages or sections, encouraging the reader to think of the experience as a guided journey rather than an open website. The language switcher, if present, is a small uppercase two-letter toggle in the corner; the secondary links, such as a "return" link in the bottom right, are understated in the same muted gray as other secondary text. The ghost chrome is the rule: no fills, no borders thicker than a pixel, no background panels behind nav items.

Media and imagery are dominated by a single hero tableau, with everything else either reduced to a typographic moment or omitted. Photography, when it appears, should be dark, low-key, and treated as if it were a still from a film rather than a marketing shot — think high contrast, deep shadows, controlled highlights, and a duotone logic where only the accent hue is allowed to break the monochrome. Three-dimensional renders, if used, should be wireframe or near-wireframe, with thin lines and minimal mass, so the visual feels constructed rather than photographed. Illustration, if used, should be linear, monochromatic, and architectural, never figurative. Grain and subtle texture are acceptable; bloom, soft glow, and color washes are not. Real images should not sit next to the hero tableau — that tableau is the only large visual on the page, and any supporting imagery below the fold should be thumbnails or icons rendered in the same thin-line system.

Standout solutions worth replicating in any topical pivot are, first, the single-accent discipline: one hue, used in at most three or four places on the page, doing the job that five colors would normally do — a call-to-action, a hero object, a status tag, and a hover state. Second, the asymmetric media-plus-text split where the visual is anchored left and low, the headline is anchored right and high, and the negative space between them is treated as composition rather than absence. Third, the integrated pagination counter that turns a sequence of pages into a guided journey and tells the reader there is more to see. Fourth, the rectangular, sharp-cornered call-to-action filled with the accent color and set in bold uppercase, which functions as the warmest element on an otherwise cold page. Fifth, the thin-line circular arrow icon that breaks the otherwise strict rectilinear geometry and gives the eye a single curved resting point. Sixth, the editorial headline treatment of large uppercase display type with wide tracking, used at a scale that lets it act as architecture rather than copy.

Things to learn from this system are, first, let a single saturated color carry the entire emotional and functional story rather than distributing energy across multiple hues. Second, integrate any sequence or timeline directly into the chrome of the page as a small counter, so progression is felt without being narrated. Third, pair every interactive surface with a clear uppercase verb — "Read the brief," "Begin the tour," "View the case" — so the action is unambiguous before the user clicks. Fourth, treat negative space as a material with weight and budget for it on the page rather than treating it as leftover. Fifth, design the hero as a single composed tableau rather than a collage of elements, so the page has a clear center of gravity.

Watch-outs are several. First, a single accent is fragile — the moment a second saturated color appears, the system collapses into visual noise, so any new component must be tested against the rule. Second, body text in muted gray on near-black sits at the borderline of legibility; the gray should be lifted to at least #B8B8B8 for small text to remain AA-compliant. Third, a thin-line circular icon next to a heavy rectangular button creates a weight mismatch, so the icon stroke should be calibrated to feel like a peer of the button rather than a hairline. Fourth, a "return" link styled in the same muted gray as captions will be read as decorative rather than functional; it needs an underline or an icon to be actionable. Fifth, a two-column hero with a large media block will not survive mobile and must be restacked vertically with the visual first or the headline first — pick deliberately. Sixth, wide letter-spacing on display type can over-expand at very large text scales, so tracking should tighten slightly as the type grows. Seventh, a small hamburger icon in the top corner needs a hit area of at least 44 pixels even if the visible glyph is much smaller. Eighth, the lone accent object in the hero is a focal-point magnet — resist adding a second warm element anywhere else on the first screen, or the eye will split and the composition will fail.

In summary, this is a dark, technical, editorial system built on a near-black field with a single saturated yellow accent, a wide-tracked uppercase display face paired with a clean grotesque body, an asymmetric media-plus-text layout with cinematic negative space, and motion that is slow, opacity-led, and editorial with entrances of roughly 300 to 600 milliseconds and hovers of 180 to 250 milliseconds on an ease-out curve. Preserve the single-accent discipline, the generous breathing room, and the strict rectilinear UI chrome whenever the system is extended into a new topical context.

bone-ochre-cinematic-duotone-giant-serif.universal_prompt:
One-liner. A high-contrast, dark-mode hero composed as a centered editorial statement, where a single saturated accent on a near-black field does the heavy lifting and everything else is restrained negative space, wide-tracked typography, and a line-based immersive backdrop.

Direction. The mood is cold, precise, technical, and quietly cinematic. The hero strategy is a slow-burning typographic moment that assumes the viewer will pause, absorb, and then make a single primary decision. Emotionally, it is doing the work of a gallery wall — a single loud object in a quiet room — rather than a marketplace. The composition leads the eye down a centered vertical axis and then opens outward into a dense, faintly rendered environment that supplies atmosphere without competing with the focal point.

Color. The palette is built on a two-tone logic: a deep neutral field plus a single saturated accent, and that logic is what must survive any thematic pivot. The background is near-black, sitting in the range of #0A0A0A to #0E0E10, anchoring the entire page as a uniform dark canvas. Surface elevations, when needed, lift only slightly into a charcoal band around #1F1F22 to #2A2A2E, used for linework, dividers, and faint environmental graphics — never for large fills. Foreground body copy reads in a light cool gray near #B8B8BD, deliberately desaturated so it never competes with the accent. The accent itself is a saturated warm yellow in the #F5E020 to #FFE600 band, used sparingly but decisively on the display word, the primary action, a thin vertical marker, and active states. The temperature story is the classic cold-warm contrast: cool dark base, warm yellow focal point, and the brain reads yellow as a tiny sun sitting on a black plane. Contrast logic puts the yellow at maximum punch against the near-black, the body gray comfortably above threshold against the field, and any additional accent (if introduced) must be kept at very low saturation or it will vibrate against the yellow. There is no gradient on text, no glow filter, no glass surface; a very subtle edge vignette is the only allowed ambient tint. If the system is extended, the rule is simple: one saturated accent, used on no more than three element classes, never as a fill behind text.

Typography. One neutral geometric grotesque family does all the work, differentiated by scale, weight, case, and tracking. The display face is a Space Grotesk-class grotesque used at an extreme size — roughly one-third of the viewport width — set in uppercase with very wide letter-spacing so the word behaves as a decorative object as much as legible text. The body face is an Inter-class grotesque set in sentence case at a small but comfortable size, with generous leading around 1.5 to 1.7. The same family, dropped to small uppercase with wide tracking, handles all chrome: top-bar labels, button labels, and the stepper. There is no secondary display face, no serif, and no monospaced font in the visible system; if a numeric or mono role is required later, it should be a quiet utility, never a second voice. The scale ratio between display and body is aggressive — roughly 8:1 to 12:1 — which is what gives the layout its editorial weight. Weight stays regular to medium; nothing is bold, and emphasis is built through size, tracking, and surrounding negative space rather than through stroke. The display word's line-height is tight; the paragraph's line-height is loose. All-caps treatments always carry wide tracking; body copy never does. The single typographic rule to preserve: the display word is the main visual accent, and its scale carries more compositional weight than its color.

Layout and composition. The page is a centered, symmetrical hero with a one-column central stack and quiet flanking elements. Vertically, the upper half is dominated by negative space; the lower half is filled by an immersive line-based environment. The central content occupies roughly the middle third of the viewport horizontally and reads in a strict top-to-bottom stack: a small top chrome strip, then display word, then paragraph, then action, then a wide lower zone of environmental graphics. The grid underneath is a standard 12-column system with content centered around the midline, and horizontal alignment between the top-left mark, the top-center stepper, and the top-right menu. Proportions of the page read as approximately 8% top chrome, 35% upper negative space with centered content, 50% immersive lower environment, and 7% bottom breathing room; these are flexible, but the airy-on-top, dense-on-bottom split is non-negotiable. Negative space is the primary design tool in the upper half and the reason the focal point reads instantly. Asymmetry is minor: a thin vertical accent bar on the upper left, a circular directional control on the right edge, and a spire-like graphic in the lower right counterbalance each other around the central axis.

Visual hierarchy. The eye hits the display word first because of its scale and isolation. Second, the body paragraph registers as supporting context directly underneath. Third, the primary action — the pill button in saturated accent — anchors the decision. Fourth, the upper-left vertical accent bar and the right-edge circular control register as supporting wayfinding. Fifth and last, the top-bar labels and stepper numerals read as chrome. Emphasis is built through scale, surrounding empty space, and saturated hue. Legibility is near-instant because there are only three vertical tiers in the central stack. The single risk to this hierarchy is the brightest node in the lower environment, which can pull attention away from the headline if it sits too close to the focal column; that node should always be dimmed or removed.

Hero treatment. The hero is a fixed-camera composition: a deep black void above, a single large typographic object at center, a short paragraph, a single action, and a faintly rendered architectural line-art environment filling the lower half like a museum tableau. The display word is framed by wide empty space on all sides, never crowded by supporting graphics. The headline is not a sentence but a word-as-object, set wide and uppercase so it reads as a label, a title, or a brand mark rather than as a call to think. The supporting paragraph sits directly below, sentence case, small, low-emphasis, never competing with the display. The action sits below the paragraph, in a pill shape, fully saturated. The lower environment reads as depth rather than content: thin lines, low opacity, monochrome, suggesting a city, a skyline, a circuit, or a constellation depending on the topic — but always as faint scaffolding behind the central statement. There is no photographic plate, no video background, and no gradient mask over the transition; the airiness of the upper half does the separation work.

Navigation and wayfinding. The primary nav is a thin top strip: a small mark on the left, a quiet stepper in the center (formatted as two numerals with a long dash, e.g. 01 — 02), and a text link plus hamburger on the right. The secondary nav is a circular outlined directional control pinned to the right edge, sized large enough to be a tap target but never competing with the central CTA. There are no breadcrumbs, no tab strips, no sidebars, and no floating menus on the hero. The stepper behaves as a position indicator rather than a control set; the right-edge circle behaves as a next/previous affordance; the hamburger behaves as a full menu escape hatch. All three secondary cues should share a single stroke weight and a single minimum radius, and none of them should ever use the saturated accent unless in an active state.

Media and imagery. Photography is absent. Imagery is built from linework, geometric primitives, and one flat saturated accent. The dominant graphic is a faint architectural or schematic line drawing that fills the lower half, rendered in a charcoal that sits only one or two values above the background — the rule is that it should be perceptible but never assertive. There is no bloom, no grain, no duotone, no halftone, and no photographic texture; the only filter in use is a low-opacity, low-saturation treatment on the linework itself. Where real images are introduced in later sections, they should sit on a near-black surface and be allowed one piece of supporting yellow at most — the environment should not have to fight the focal object for the accent. Illustrations, if any, follow the same flat, geometric, monochrome-with-accent rule as the hero.

Standout solutions. First, the single-accent-on-black rule: reserve the saturated yellow for no more than three element classes (the display word, the primary action, and an active or wayfinding marker), and never use it as a fill behind text. Second, the display-word-as-object: a single grotesque word set in wide-tracked uppercase at extreme scale, carrying the composition through typographic mass rather than color. Third, the centered vertical reading stack: display, paragraph, action, in that order, with generous leading and a single column. Fourth, the top chrome triplet: mark left, stepper center, menu right, all set in tiny uppercase with wide tracking — a quiet gallery-label system rather than a navigation bar. Fifth, the right-edge circular directional control as a soft secondary cue, never louder than the CTA. Sixth, the immersive lower-half line environment: full-bleed, low-opacity, monochrome, functioning as atmosphere rather than content.

Things to learn from. Let one element carry the color story; do not spread the accent across the page. Use negative space in the upper half as a premium signal and let the lower half supply density. Make the display word do double duty as both the brand voice and the layout anchor. Tie every interactive node to a labeled verb or numeral so chrome never has to be decoded. Keep the entire motion vocabulary to opacity, small translate-up, and restrained scale, all on a single ease-out curve.

Watch-outs. The brightest node in the lower environment can pull the eye away from the headline and should be dimmed or moved. A right-edge directional control with too little weight will read as decoration; give it a minimum tap target and consider an active-state color shift. Paragraph text set small and gray-on-black is the most marginal element for contrast and should be tested at body sizes, not just at scale. Two greens of similar value, or any second saturated hue near the yellow, will cause color vibration; never introduce a competing warm. A top-center stepper that is too quiet becomes useless as orientation; keep numerals legible. Icons without labels will be ambiguous in this restrained palette; pair every glyph with a word. Focal-point crowding happens fast when the lower environment creeps too high; preserve the empty band above the display word. Reduced-motion users must still receive the core hierarchy, so any parallax, letter-reveal, or scale-up animation needs an opacity-only fallback.

Animation. The motion personality is smooth, inertial, and minimal. The first screen fades the display word in with a 12 to 20 pixel translate-up over 600 to 900 milliseconds, optionally word-by-word, then brings the paragraph in 300 milliseconds later, then the button in another 200 milliseconds later with a small scale from 0.96 to 1. The top chrome fades in immediately or within the first 200 milliseconds. The lower environment drifts continuously at roughly 0.3 to 0.5 pixels per frame to suggest depth without distraction; the upper-left vertical accent bar stays static as an anchor. Scroll-driven reveals are limited to a soft fade plus 16 to 24 pixel translate-up, staggered 60 to 100 milliseconds between siblings, with subtle parallax between foreground and midground layers of the line environment. Pinning is avoided because it fights the airy editorial pacing. Hover and micro-interactions are restrained: the button scales to 1.03 with a brightness shift over about 180 milliseconds, the circular control scales to 1.08 and shifts its stroke to the accent on hover, links animate an underline offset over about 160 milliseconds, and the active stepper numeral shifts from gray to the accent. Effects are never stacked — one transform and one color shift at most. Technical rules: use transform and opacity, never animate blur across large areas, never move body text, and respect prefers-reduced-motion by disabling parallax and shortening all reveals to opacity-only fades. Easing is a single curve family: cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1) for entrances, cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1) for state changes, and a soft spring only on the primary action.

Visual scenario. The interface is built for a thoughtful, single-decision entry moment on a wide desktop canvas. The session is short — the screen is a gateway, not a workspace — and the page tolerates a strong opening statement because there is only one thing to do. On smaller screens the centered reading order, the display-word prominence, the accent role, the action accessibility, and the contrast ratios must be preserved; below 768 pixels the lower environment should become denser and lower in opacity, the display word should scale fluidly with a clamp function, the top chrome should collapse to mark plus menu, and paragraph line length should hold near 60 to 70 characters.

Summary. A high-contrast dark hero on a single-accent palette, organized as a centered editorial composition with one large wide-tracked display word, a short paragraph, a single saturated pill action, and a faint line-art environment filling the lower half. The system runs on typographic scale and negative space; the accent is used sparingly; the chrome is gallery-quiet; the motion vocabulary is opacity, small translate-up, restrained scale, and one ease-out curve. What must survive any thematic pivot: the two-tone color logic, the centered reading order, the generous upper-half breathing room, the display word as compositional anchor, and the single primary action.
